excerpt_original: From Cynthia Erivo’s bravura barrister to Johnny Depp’s surprisingly good Scrooge, take a quick glance at this week’s new films *** Continue reading...

blocks.alt: Cynthia Erivo and Daniel Ings in Prima Facie.
blocks.caption: Charged … Cynthia Erivo and Daniel Ings in Prima Facie. Photograph: Nicola Dove Photographer/Nicola Dove

blocks.text: Prima Facie ★★★★☆
In a sentence Screen adaptation of Suzie Miller’s international stage hit stars Cynthia Erivo as a lawyer whose career defending rape suspects is undermined by experience.
What our reviewer said “A blazingly fierce, effortlessly commanding central performance from Erivo, like something from classical drama, powers the movie.” Peter Bradshaw

blocks.alt: Vincent Munier’s father in the Vosges Forest.
blocks.caption: Human nature … Vincent Munier’s father in the Vosges forest. Photograph: Vincent Munier

blocks.text: Whispers in the Woods ★★★★☆
In a sentence Director Vincent Munier takes his father and son into the Vosges forest in France in an emotional study of human-animal interaction.

What our reviewer said “A subtle, tender work that evokes the need to pass on interest and engagement in the natural world to younger generations, but which manages to avoid feeling too preachy or sanctimonious.” Leslie Felperin

blocks.alt: David Wilkinson receives his regular chemotherapy treatment.
blocks.caption: Unselfconscious. … David Wilkinson at his regular chemotherapy appointment

blocks.text: In a sentence David Wilkinson’s compassionate film deals with his own bowel cancer treatment, and asks why so many much younger people are getting the same diagnosis.

What our reviewer said “This is a sobering but very compassionate, humorous, generous film, and one that shows how Wilkinson’s highly personal and unselfconsciously confessional style has grown into something very watchable and distinctive.” Peter Bradshaw

blocks.alt: Soraya Akhlaghi on her flight from Iran.
blocks.caption: Flight of invention … Soraya Akhlaghi on her flight from Iran. Photograph: Oskouei Films

blocks.text: A Fox Under a Pink Moon ★★★★☆
In a sentence Refugee Soraya Akhlaghi filmed her perilous flight from Iran and precarious new life over five years on her phone, reassembled here with boldly imaginative animations.
What our reviewer said “A born creator, Akhlaghi channels her struggles and despair into florid, intense drawings.” Phuong Le

blocks.alt: The US army’s first Black special ops team.
blocks.caption: The US army’s first Black special ops team, in Soul Patrol. Photograph: Kino Lorber

blocks.text: Soul Patrol ★★★★☆
In a sentence Story of the US army’s first Black special ops team at work in Vietnam, relating the incredible bravery they showed in the face of battle and unrelenting bigotry.

What our reviewer said “The title of course refers to the soul music that became anthemic to these soldiers, but also, with grim irony, to their sense that their souls had died in the jungle, fighting people they felt were just like them.” Peter Bradshaw

blocks.caption: Ferocious … Billie Jean King in 1974. Photograph: Ellen Griesedieck

blocks.text: Give Me the Ball! ★★★★☆
In a sentence Sparky and engaging documentary about tennis ace Billie Jean King, who fought her whole career to ensure the women’s game got the respect it deserved.
What our reviewer said “King was a ferocious force in women’s tennis from the 60s onwards and a vehement but polite advocate for equal rights on prize money.” Peter Bradshaw

blocks.alt: Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley and Johnny Depp in Ebenezer.
blocks.caption: Scrooge news … Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley and Johnny Depp in Ebenezer. Photograph: Jaap Buitendijk

blocks.text: Ebenezer ★★★☆☆
In a sentence Johnny Depp stars as the celebrated miser who finds redemption in a new version of the Dickens classic A Christmas Carol.

What our reviewer said “As Scrooge, Depp is in fact rather good; theatrically bad-tempered and petulant and, as with his Jack Sparrow, I suspect Depp’s comedy timing and sonorous British accent might have been learned from his old Fast Show comrade Paul Whitehouse.” Peter Bradshaw

blocks.alt: Traces of Justice, the latest film from Chen Sicheng.
blocks.caption: Apt pupil … Traces of Justice, the latest film from Chen Sicheng. Photograph: Trinity/CineAsia

blocks.text: Traces of Justice ★★★☆☆
In a sentence Forensic scientist Cui Daozhi, the “Chinese Sherlock Holmes”, is the real-life central figure of a cop thriller that ranges across 30 years of gripping cases.
What our reviewer said “The latest from Chen Sicheng, prime mover behind the hit Detective Chinatown franchise, offers a disarming mix of propaganda, copaganda and gripping narrative.” Mike McCahill

blocks.caption: Grace under fire … The Mosquito Bowl. Photograph: Kane Skennar/Netfllix ©2026

blocks.text: The Mosquito Bowl ★★★☆☆
In a sentence Peter Berg directs a handsomely made second world war drama about an American football game before the battle of Okinawa.

What our reviewer said “Berg has a knack for grace within visual cacophony and chaos; graphic sequences in battle and from the 1944 Christmas Eve pickup game at Guadalcanal that gives the film its name suggest, far more than its anvil-heavy dialogue, the connections between the gridiron and the battlefield.” Adrian Horton

blocks.alt: Kunsang Kyirong’s debut feature film, 100 Sunset.
blocks.caption: Kunsang Kyirong’s debut feature film, 100 Sunset. Photograph: Day for Night

blocks.text: 100 Sunset ★★★☆☆
In a sentence Kunsang Kyirong’s debut feature is an elliptical, elusive drama that follows Kunsel, an introverted woman, through Toronto’s tight-knit Tibetan community.
What our reviewer said “In the end, the film fades like a vapour trail in the sky, its mood of disorientation and dislocation perhaps a reflection of Kunsel’s state of mind.” Cath Clarke
Fjord ★★☆☆☆
In a sentence Cristian Mungiu won his second Palme d’Or with this disquieting child abuse drama starring Renate Reinsve and Sebastian Stan.

What our reviewer said “Ultimately, the film does not compellingly deliver a blazing truth about its various relationships – but neither does it intriguingly withhold any such truth from us.” Peter Bradshaw

blocks.alt: Nicholas Hoult as Ryan in How to rob a bank.
blocks.caption: Not that rich … Nicholas Hoult as Ryan in How to Rob a Bank. Photograph: Megan Schoenbachler/Amazon MGM Studios

blocks.text: How to Rob a Bank ★★☆☆☆
In a sentence Nicholas Hoult, Anna Sawai and Pete Davidson play Robin Hood in an anti-capitalist caper movie that attempts to mix social commentary with action.

What our reviewer said “For a film that’s supposed to enrage and excite and energise, it’s all strangely, boringly flat and with a runtime stretching past two hours, surprisingly sluggish too.” Benjamin Lee
Re-released this week

blocks.alt: David Bowie in the Man Who Fell to Earth.
blocks.caption: Authentically alien … David Bowie in The Man Who Fell to Earth. Photograph: Cinetext/British Lion/Allstar

blocks.text: The Man Who Fell to Earth ★★★★★

links.text: The Man Who Fell to Earth

blocks.text: In a sentence David Bowie plays an intergalactic visitor who becomes a successful tech entrepreneur in Nicolas Roeg’s 1976 sci-fi story.

What our reviewer said “There is an extraordinary sui generis central performance by David Bowie, whose unselfconscious gentleness and vulnerability now look very moving and bizarrely authentic in a way that they didn’t in 1976.” Peter Bradshaw

blocks.caption: Dock briefs … Tilda Swinton in Female Perversions. Photograph: MUBI

blocks.text: Female Perversions ★★★★★
In a sentence Tilda Swinton’s first US film, from 1996, in which she plays a lawyer who searches for erotic adventures in a rework of Madame Bovary.

What our reviewer said “It’s an amazingly unselfconscious performance which marked her out as quite unlike any other female lead, all but impossible to cast in boilerplate Hollywood cinema.” Peter Bradshaw

blocks.caption: Revolutionary … Kirsten Dunst as Marie Antoinette. Photograph: 11Leigh Johns/Columbia Pictures/Allstar

blocks.text: Marie Antoinette ★★★☆☆
In a sentence Sofia Coppola’s biopic of the French queen, combining dazzling visual tableaux and formal set pieces in strict period, with new wave chart hits from the 1970s and 80s.
What our reviewer said “Coppola’s presentation of Marie’s life has a sisterly, unjudging intimacy, and the director has carried off pert inventions and provocations with some style.” Peter Bradshaw
Film
